touches.text: `cairn codemother retire <path>...` does the deletion. It runs the proofs of the files that name the target, before and after moving it aside. A proof that turns red is a caller, and the target goes back. Why? Running a proof tells a caller from a mention; reading the text cannot.
On every Windows box, what Cairn starts runs without a console window by default; a window opens only when someone asks for one. WHY: the boxes serve him (the media box showed pop-ups during videos).
INTENTION:
import_sieve: one parse of every .py into an import graph; what reaches what. WHY: enforces "only the proxy reaches the host/database" and RULE 1 by physics. USERS: CodeMother, the inference proxy.

RULE 1, ENCAPSULATION: every component talks to every other only through that component's public interface: a device's is the bus plus any client tool it publishes; a machine's or tool's is what its entry declares. Nothing outside a device reaches into its code, skills included. A ticket builds inside its own component, and its proofs measure only that component. WHY: it limits a change to the component that made it.

What the waker starts outlives whoever started it (detached, or through systemd-run --user, which gives it its own memory cap and log while still deciding nothing). Restarting a shim never takes down the bus it once woke.
Nothing requires Akien's word for a proof to run. A proof that starts Windows processes runs without asking; no env var or standing flag gates it.
Owns the inspectors and gates (9.4): everything in the code pipeline that checks. The exception is diagnostic_inspector, which is base's (17.1).

Hollow runs: proves a proof goes red when the build is removed.
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
A proof that cannot go red without its build (its hollow is empty) stands only on Akien's answered approval, recorded as the hollow reading and re-read at clearance; any other empty hollow is red.
build_inspector

Where a tool lives: the general collection, cairn/tools/, is the default. A tool goes with its holder (cairn/devices/<d>/tools/) only when nothing else could ever use it (a tool for a part only that one device has). If there is any chance somebody else might want it, it goes in the general collection.

A client tool a device publishes (2.3.7.1) is not the general case: it is the device's own interface, made for other components to use, so it lives with its device (cairn/devices/<d>/tools/<t>/, published_by_device). Scratch bus, the database client, the trouble store, the librarian's trees and the system device's host tool all live there. CC's decision, from 2.3.7.1 and Akien's "hostname should come from the system device" (2026-11-21). - akiendelllinux_cc_0
CP4 Make everything suck less for everybody. Reduce friction for ALL affected beings: living beings, ecosystems, AIs. The terminal goal.

A retirement checks its callers in the same act as the deletion: nothing imports the module being deleted, and nothing runs the command or path being deleted. A file that only names it (a fixture, a record, a charter) is not a caller. Nothing checks afterwards. Why? Naming is history; only a caller breaks, and a caller that comes later breaks loudly on its own. A standing proof that a thing stays gone is history kept as code.
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Test tiers: commit, hourly, daily and weekly. Each tier runs only what it must, so a commit needs only its own proofs and the long runs wait for the long tiers; nothing runs just in case.

Reds don't get lost. Each run writes a ticket for every new red it finds and every orphaned file it sees, unless one is already open for it. A red seen in passing gets the same treatment. Every red and every orphaned file is fixed; one unrelated to the work in hand is ticketed, and once it is, that crossing can go ahead.

The RULE 1 check is a path check: code inside device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo (anything not under cairn.devices.bar), except a tool foo publishes (cairn.devices.foo.tools.<x>, its charter saying published_by_device). Inside one device there is one owner, so nothing is checked there. A charter's public_interface describes what the component offers (modules, functions, bus verbs, commands); the check does not read it. WHY: a path check is the simplest thing the code can test.
Physics: the encapsulation_holds sieve in build_inspector, a device-path check. Code in device bar may not import cairn.devices.foo except a tool foo publishes. Inside one device nothing is checked.
